summary: Specifies a profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 4, an experimental variant using TFRC-SP, which suits applications sending small packets. CCID 4 is for experimental use.

eli5.summary: If you send tiny messages, you must be careful not to flood a road. This is a speed rule designed for senders of tiny messages.

questions: what is the dccp dropped packets option
how does ccid 4 differ from ccid 3
subtitle: DCCP congestion control for senders of small packets, built on TFRC-SP and kept deliberately experimental.

tldr.problem: Applications that send small packets, such as streaming media, want a TCP-friendly sending rate without abrupt rate changes, but packet header overhead makes plain TFRC unfair for them.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 4 is CCID 3 with the TFRC-SP changes: the rate is reduced by a header-size factor, packets are at least 10 ms apart, short loss intervals count actual losses, and a new Dropped Packets option reports those counts.
tldr.outcome: CCID 4 is experimental because TFRC-SP is experimental, and it is not proposed for widespread deployment in the global Internet. RFC 6323 and RFC 8311 later updated it.

today: RFC 5622 is an Experimental RFC and has been updated by RFC 6323 and RFC 8311. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: CCID 4 in Brief
sections.content:
RFC 5622 defines Congestion Control Identifier 4 (CCID 4) for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340). It is a modified version of CCID 3 from RFC 4342, and it assumes the reader already knows CCID 3.

CCID 3 uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). CCID 4 instead uses TFRC-SP from RFC 4828, an experimental small-packet variant. The goal is roughly the same bandwidth in bits per second as a TCP flow using packets of up to 1500 bytes under the same level of congestion.

Like CCID 3, it suits flows that want to avoid abrupt changes in sending rate, such as streaming media with small or moderate receiver buffering. The application may use a small fixed segment size or vary the size as the allowed rate changes. CCID 4 does not dictate the size.
sections.eli5: CCID 4 is a speed rule for programs that send many tiny messages. It copies an older speed rule and adjusts it so tiny messages are treated fairly.

sections.title: How CCID 4 Differs from CCID 3
sections.content:
The RFC lists exactly four differences from CCID 3, all taken from TFRC-SP.

  • Header size: the allowed rate in bytes per second is reduced by a factor for header size. Headers are estimated at 36 bytes (20 for IPv4 and 16 for the DCCP-Data header with 48-bit sequence numbers), or 32 bytes with 24-bit sequence numbers. For N-byte data packets the rate is reduced by N/(N+36).
  • Maximum sending rate: the sender enforces a minimum interval of 10 ms between data packets. If scheduling granularity makes that impractical, up to one extra packet MAY be sent per timeslice, with no more than three packets in any 30 ms.
  • Short loss intervals: for loss intervals of at most two round-trip times, the loss rate counts actual packets lost or marked. With N data packets and K lost or marked, the interval length is N/K instead of N.
  • Nominal segment size: the TCP throughput equation uses 1460 bytes.

Everything else, including slow-start and feedback packets, works exactly as in CCID 3. Connection establishment follows Section 4 of RFC 4342, and RFC 4828 is normative except where the RFC says otherwise.
sections.eli5: Think of a mail rule where each envelope costs a bit of space. Tiny letters waste more space on envelopes, so the rule slows them a little and spaces them out, and it counts every lost letter in a bad stretch.

sections.title: A Half-Connection in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC gives an informative example of one half-connection. The sender transmits DCCP-Data packets at the allowed transmit rate. Each carries a sequence number and a window counter in the CCVal field, which the receiver uses to decide when several losses belong to one loss event. On an ECN-capable half-connection they are sent with the ECT(0) or ECT(1) codepoint.

The receiver returns DCCP-Ack packets at least once per round-trip time, unless the sender sends less than one packet per round-trip time. These carry feedback about recent loss intervals. The sender updates its allowed rate from this feedback, using RFC 5348 and RFC 4828. It can compute the loss event rate itself, or use one the receiver calculates and reports.

The sender also estimates round-trip times and computes a nofeedback time. If no feedback arrives in that time (at least four round-trip times), it halves its sending rate.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps sending at a safe speed while the receiver sends back notes about what got lost. If the notes stop coming, the sender cuts its speed in half.

sections.title: Options and the Dropped Packets Option
sections.content:
CCID 4 imports the CCID 3 options and features, each carrying the same data and read the same way. Table 1 of the RFC lists option types 192 (Loss Event Rate, length 6), 193 (Loss Intervals, variable), 194 (Receive Rate, length 6) and 195 (Dropped Packets, variable). All CCID 4 options MUST be ignored on DCCP-Data packets. The Send Loss Event Rate feature is number 192.

The new piece is the Dropped Packets option. The existing Loss Intervals option reports the length of each loss interval, but TFRC-SP also needs the number of packets lost or marked in it. The option lists one 24-bit Drop Count per loss interval, for one to 84 consecutive intervals, newest first. A Drop Count MUST NOT exceed the interval's Loss Length.

Receivers MUST send Dropped Packets options with every feedback packet, and any packet with a Loss Intervals option MUST also carry one covering the same intervals. If the option is missing, a sender computing the loss event rate itself MUST treat the Drop Counts as equal to the Loss Lengths. The receiver can spot short loss intervals with the window counter, which the sender raises by 1 every quarter of a round-trip time. This can give false positives, which the RFC illustrates.
sections.eli5: The old note says how long each bad stretch was. The new note also says how many letters were lost in it, so the sender can judge how bad things really were.

sections.title: Why the Field Sizes Stayed Large
sections.content:
Section 11 explains a design choice. CCID 4 could have used smaller fields, since its sender enforces a 10 ms minimum gap between packets. The Loss Intervals option keeps CCID 3's three-byte fields to minimize implementation differences between the two. A two-byte Data Length field reports up to 65,536 packets, enough for round-trip times of at most 2.5 seconds, so longer round-trip times need three bytes.

For the Dropped Packets option, a one-byte count would allow 255 and a two-byte count 65,535. A one-byte field would probably suffice, since more than 255 losses in an interval needs a round-trip time over 2.55 seconds, though round-trip times above three seconds are not unusual on satellite links. The RFC still specifies three bytes for consistency with the Loss Intervals option.
sections.eli5: The designers could have used smaller boxes for the numbers. They kept the bigger boxes so the new rule looks like the old one and is easy to build.

sections.title: Status, Security and IANA
sections.content:
CCID 4 is experimental because TFRC-SP is. RFC 4828 explains why TFRC-SP is not intended for widespread deployment in the global Internet at this time. If a Standards-Track RFC changes the status of TFRC-SP, CCID 4 should be updated to match.

Security considerations are those of Section 11 of RFC 4342, and CCID 4 introduces no new ones. IANA is asked for the value 4 in the DCCP CCID namespace, a permanent codepoint so experiments across the Internet can use different codebases. The RFC allocates option types 192 to 195 and feature number 192, and reserves 184-190 and 248-254 for experimental and testing use.
sections.eli5: This speed rule is still a test, so it is not meant for the whole internet yet. It adds no new safety worries beyond the older rule.

fields.name: Drop Count
fields.desc: Packets lost or ECN-marked in one loss interval; more counts may follow.
